summary: For ages 7-8, build the habit of looking for structure before computing or naming: ask 'what do I already know that this is like?' Three strands: (1) read a whole multiplication/division fact family off one array (6×4, 4×6, 24÷4, 24÷6 from the same 6 rows of 4); (2) use three-digit place value so adding 100/10/1 changes only the matching column, barring a carry into the next place; (3) classify shapes by properties (sides, right angles, parallel pairs) so the classification survives rotation. This is the run-up to the distributive property (7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3) and to reasoning about figures by structure.
misconceptions: Treats multiplication and division as unrelated, recomputing 24÷4 from scratch despite knowing 6×4
When adding 100 to a three-digit number, changes the wrong column or mis-carries
Classifies shapes by orientation/appearance (a rotated square becomes a 'diamond'; only a 'pointing-up' triangle is a triangle)
Thinks a derived fact must be checked by counting because facts feel separate rather than connected

activities.title: One array, four facts
steps: Lay out 24 counters as 6 rows of 4 and state the multiplication it shows (6×4=24).
Rotate the whole array a quarter turn and read it again as 4 rows of 6; say why 6×4 and 4×6 are the same 24 dots seen two ways.
Cover one factor: with 24 shared into 4 rows, read off how many are in each row (6) to get 24÷4; then read 24÷6 the same way.
Say in your own words how knowing 6×4=24 means you already know 24÷4 and 24÷6 without counting.
Try a second fact family (e.g. 5 rows of 3) and derive all four facts from the single array.
activities.insight: One rectangular array holds a whole fact family; multiplication and division are the same structure read different ways, so a known product gives the related quotients without recomputing.

activities.title: Partition to derive a harder product
steps: Take a product you don't know by heart, e.g. 7×8, and lay it as 7 rows of 8.
Split the 8 columns into 5 and 3, drawing a line through the array.
Work out the two easier parts (7×5=35 and 7×3=21) and add them (35+21=56).
State the rule you used: 7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3, then try splitting a different product your own way.
activities.insight: A large product can be built from easier known products by partitioning the array — this is the distributive property seen concretely.

activities.title: Predict which column moves
steps: Using a three-digit place-value apparatus or arrow cards, build a number such as 253 (or 470).
Before adding, predict out loud which digit will change and which will stay the same when you add 100.
Add one hundred-flat (or spin the +100 wheel) and check: for 253 and 470 only the hundreds count moves, with no carry.

Repeat for +10 and +1, each time predicting first, then stating why only that one column changed (true for 253 or 470; if the column being added to holds a 9, notice that a carry also changes the next place).
activities.insight: Place value is structured by columns; adding 100 changes only the hundreds, 10 only the tens, and 1 only the ones, unless the addition causes a carry into the next place (e.g. 259+1=260, 295+10=305, 970+100=1070).

activities.title: Classify by properties, not by how it looks
steps: Pick a shape and run a property checklist: count the sides, mark the right angles, find any parallel pairs.
Classify it from the checklist (e.g. square: 4 equal sides, 4 right angles, 2 pairs of parallel sides — also a rectangle).
Rotate the shape 45° and re-run the checklist; confirm the same properties, so the classification does not change.
Sort several shapes into overlapping sets (e.g. 'has a right angle', 'has parallel sides') and place a rotated square and an upside-down triangle correctly.
Justify one classification aloud by citing properties, not orientation.
activities.insight: A shape's class comes from its properties (sides, angles, parallel lines), which stay the same under rotation — a tilted square is still a square; calling it a 'diamond' does not make it a different shape (a square is also a special rhombus).

checkQuestion: You know that 6 × 4 = 24. Without counting anything out, what does that tell you about 4 × 6, and about 24 ÷ 4 and 24 ÷ 6? How does the one fact give you the others?
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child deriving all three from the one fact and explaining the link: 4×6 is the same array turned round; 24÷4 asks how many fours in 24 (six), 24÷6 asks how many sixes (four) — division undoes the multiplication.
